cards.front: What is a TPU in one sentence?
cards.back: A Google-designed ASIC for accelerating neural-network matrix multiplications, built around a systolic array and high-bandwidth on-package memory.

cards.front: Who designed and manufactures the TPU?
cards.back: Google designs it; foundry partners (e.g., TSMC, Samsung) fabricate the silicon.

cards.front: What problem class do TPUs accelerate best?
cards.back: Dense matrix multiply / accumulate (MAC) heavy workloads — feed-forward layers, attention QKV projections, embeddings. Not great for sparse / branchy code.

cards.front: What does MXU stand for?
cards.back: Matrix X (multiply) Unit — the systolic array that does the heavy linear algebra.

cards.front: What does VPU stand for in the TPU context?
cards.back: Vector Processing Unit — handles activations, reductions, softmax, and other element-wise / control-light ops the MXU can't.

cards.front: What does HBM stand for?
cards.back: High Bandwidth Memory — DRAM stacked on the same package as the chip, connected via wide silicon interposer.

cards.front: What does ICI stand for?
cards.back: Inter-Chip Interconnect — Google's point-to-point links between TPU chips inside a pod.

cards.front: What does OCS stand for in TPU v4+?
cards.back: Optical Circuit Switch — reconfigures the 3D-torus topology of a pod in software, no rewiring.

cards.front: What does XLA stand for?
cards.back: Accelerated Linear Algebra — the Google compiler that lowers JAX/TF/PyTorch ops to TPU instructions.

cards.front: What is a "systolic array"?
cards.back: A 2-D grid of simple MAC units that pass data in a rhythmic, pipelined fashion (heartbeat) — operands stream in, partial sums march out, almost no register-file or memory access per cycle.

cards.front: Why is a systolic array more energy-efficient than a GPU for dense matmul?
cards.back: Data moves locally between adjacent cells instead of going through a large register file or shared memory each cycle. Local wires = ~10–100× less energy per op than long wires.

cards.front: In weight-stationary dataflow, what stays put and what streams?
cards.back: Weights are pre-loaded and stay in their MAC cells; activations stream in horizontally; partial sums propagate vertically.

cards.front: In output-stationary dataflow, what stays put?
cards.back: The partial-sum accumulator stays in each cell; both operands (weights and activations) stream through.

cards.front: What is the pipeline-fill cost of an N×N systolic array running K-deep matmul?
cards.back: Roughly K + 2N − 2 cycles (fill + drain bubble). For small K relative to N the bubble dominates utilization.

cards.front: For a 128×128 array and K=512, what is the fill cost?
cards.back: K + 2N − 2 = 512 + 256 − 2 = 766 cycles. Useful work = 512 cycles → ~67% utilization on a single matmul of that shape.

cards.front: What were the MXU dimensions of TPU v1?
cards.back: A single 256×256 INT8 MXU. One big array, inference-only, no floating point.

cards.front: What numeric format did TPU v1 use?
cards.back: INT8 (quantized integer). Designed for serving, not training.

cards.front: What were the MXU dimensions of TPU v2 (and v3)?
cards.back: Two 128×128 MXUs per core, BF16 multiply with FP32 accumulate. First TPU that could TRAIN, not just infer.

cards.front: Why did Google move from one 256×256 MXU (v1) to two 128×128 MXUs (v2+)?
cards.back: Better utilization on smaller batch / smaller-matmul shapes; one big array stalls badly when M, N, or K < array dim. Two smaller arrays = finer-grained packing.

cards.front: What is bfloat16's bit layout?
cards.back: 1 sign + 8 exponent + 7 mantissa = 16 bits total. Same dynamic range as FP32, half the mantissa precision.

cards.front: What is FP16's bit layout?
cards.back: 1 sign + 5 exponent + 10 mantissa = 16 bits. More precision than BF16 but much narrower dynamic range → frequent over/underflow in training.

cards.front: Why is BF16 preferred over FP16 for neural-network training?
cards.back: BF16 keeps FP32's dynamic range (8-bit exponent), so gradients don't underflow during back-prop. FP16's 5-bit exponent forces loss-scaling tricks that BF16 avoids.

cards.front: What is the standard multiply/accumulate precision combo on TPUs?
cards.back: Multiply in BF16, accumulate in FP32. Cheaper compute on the multiply, drift-resistant sum on the accumulator.

cards.front: What HBM did TPU v2 use, and how much?
cards.back: First TPU with HBM — 8 GiB of HBM, ~600 GB/s.

cards.front: What HBM and capacity did TPU v4 use?
cards.back: 32 GiB of HBM2, ~1.2 TB/s bandwidth.

cards.front: What HBM and capacity does TPU v5p use?
cards.back: HBM3, up to 192 GiB per chip, multi-TB/s bandwidth.

cards.front: What is "on-chip SRAM" called on a TPU and who manages it?
cards.back: VMEM (and a few smaller buffers). It is a software-managed scratchpad — XLA explicitly decides what lives there. Unlike a CPU cache, there is no hardware replacement policy.

cards.front: Why does software-managed SRAM (VMEM) win over a hardware cache on a TPU?
cards.back: Deterministic latency, no thrashing, perfectly predictable for the compiler. Hardware caches help unpredictable workloads — neural-network kernels are highly predictable, so cache management overhead is pure waste.

cards.front: What are the four main on-chip components of a modern TPU core?
cards.back: MXU (matrix multiply), VPU (vector), scalar unit (control), and VMEM (software-managed SRAM scratchpad).

cards.front: Roughly how many ICI links does each TPU v4 chip have?
cards.back: 6 ICI links per chip, enabling a 3-D torus topology.

cards.front: What is the topology of a TPU v4 pod?
cards.back: A 3-D torus reconfigured by Optical Circuit Switches (OCS), so the logical topology can match the workload (data-parallel ring vs. model-parallel mesh).

cards.front: What is a "slice" in TPU terminology?
cards.back: A contiguous, statically-allocated subset of a TPU pod (e.g., 2×2×2 = 8 chips), with its own ICI fabric carved out by OCS.

cards.front: What is a "multislice" job?
cards.back: A job spanning multiple pod slices, stitched together over the slower Data Center Network (DCN) instead of ICI. Used when one slice isn't big enough.

cards.front: Why does the OCS matter for multi-tenant scheduling?
cards.back: It lets the data center physically re-wire the topology per job in software, in milliseconds, so different shaped slices can coexist without fragmentation.

cards.front: What does "data parallelism" mean for TPU training?
cards.back: The same model is replicated on each chip; each replica processes a different mini-batch shard; gradients are all-reduced over ICI.

cards.front: What does "model parallelism" mean for TPU training?
cards.back: The model's parameters are split across chips. Each chip holds a slice of the weights and only computes its piece of the forward / backward pass.

cards.front: What does "pipeline parallelism" mean?
cards.back: The model is split layer-by-layer across chips. Micro-batches flow through the pipeline so multiple chips work simultaneously on different micro-batches at different layers.

cards.front: What is the all-reduce operation, and why is it the dominant collective in training?
cards.back: Sum (or average) of a tensor across all chips, with the result broadcast back to each. Gradient averaging in data-parallel training requires an all-reduce after every backward pass.

cards.front: What ring-algorithm time does all-reduce take on N chips with tensor size B?
cards.back: Approximately 2(N−1)/N · B / bandwidth. For large N this approaches 2B / bandwidth regardless of N — bandwidth-bound, not latency-bound.

cards.front: What is JAX's "pmap" used for on TPUs?
cards.back: Single-program-multiple-data parallelism: replicate a function across all devices in a slice; each replica gets its own shard of the input.

cards.front: What is JAX's "shard_map" used for?
cards.back: Explicit, fine-grained sharding control: you specify the mesh axes and partition spec per tensor. Lower-level alternative to pjit's automatic sharding.

cards.front: What is XLA's main job in the TPU stack?
cards.back: Lower a high-level computation graph (HLO) into TPU instructions: fuse ops, allocate VMEM, schedule MXU/VPU/DMA, generate the explicit dataflow program.

cards.front: What is "op fusion" and why does XLA care about it?
cards.back: Combining adjacent ops (e.g., matmul → bias-add → ReLU) into a single kernel that keeps intermediate results in VMEM/registers, avoiding HBM round-trips. HBM round-trips dominate cost for memory-bound ops.

cards.front: What is the "roofline model" for accelerator performance?
cards.back: Performance is bounded by the minimum of peak compute and operational intensity × peak bandwidth. Plot FLOPs/byte on x-axis vs. achievable FLOP/s on y-axis to see whether a kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound.

cards.front: For BF16 matmul, what is the operational intensity threshold above which you are compute-bound on a typical TPU?
cards.back: Roughly FLOPs / byte ≥ peak_compute / peak_bandwidth. For TPU v4 (~275 TFLOPs BF16, ~1.2 TB/s HBM) the ridge ≈ 230 FLOPs/byte. Below that → memory-bound.

cards.front: What is "weight rematerialization" (recompute) and when do you use it?
cards.back: Re-running parts of the forward pass during the backward pass to avoid storing all activations. Trades extra compute for reduced HBM use — essential when sequence length × batch size doesn't fit in HBM.

cards.front: What is gradient checkpointing?
cards.back: Same idea as rematerialization — keep activations only at a few "checkpoint" boundaries, recompute the rest during backward. Cuts activation memory by ~√N for an N-layer network.

cards.front: What is "FSDP" (Fully Sharded Data Parallel)?
cards.back: Each chip holds only 1/N of the parameters, optimizer state, and gradients. Parameters are all-gathered just before they're needed, then released. Trades extra communication for massive memory savings.

cards.front: Why is FSDP attractive on TPUs?
cards.back: ICI bandwidth is high enough that the extra all-gather/reduce-scatter traffic is affordable, and HBM is the binding constraint on what model size fits per chip. FSDP lets you train 10× larger models per pod.

cards.front: What is the difference between a "step" and a "training step" on a TPU pod?
cards.back: A single optimization step (forward + backward + optimizer apply) is a "training step." Internally it may contain many compiled XLA steps if microbatching or gradient accumulation is used.

cards.front: What does "double-buffering" mean in TPU DMA?
cards.back: Two HBM-to-VMEM transfers in flight at once — while the MXU computes on buffer A, DMA fills buffer B. Hides memory latency behind compute.

cards.front: How does the TPU host (CPU) talk to the TPU chip?
cards.back: Via PCIe. The host enqueues compiled XLA programs and shovels initial data; from then on the TPUs talk among themselves over ICI.

cards.front: Why are TPUs typically not used for graph neural networks or sparse models?
cards.back: Their MXU is optimized for dense matmul. Sparse / pointer-heavy / dynamic-shape workloads under-utilize the array and suffer DMA stalls. GPUs (with finer-grained scheduling) often win there.

cards.front: Why do TPUs prefer static shapes?
cards.back: XLA must fully lay out the dataflow program at compile time; dynamic shapes force re-compilation or padding. Padding to a power-of-two batch / sequence dim is the common workaround.

cards.front: What is the canonical "padding to multiples of 128" rule on TPUs?
cards.back: Inputs to the MXU should have dimensions that are multiples of 128 (the MXU side length on v2+). Non-multiples are auto-padded by XLA, wasting compute.

cards.front: What is "loss scaling" and is it needed with BF16?
cards.back: A trick to multiply the loss by a large constant so small FP16 gradients don't underflow. With BF16 it is NOT needed because BF16 has FP32's exponent range.

cards.front: What is the "all-gather" collective?
cards.back: Each chip starts with a shard of a tensor; all chips end up with the full concatenated tensor. Inverse of all-to-all-scatter; used in FSDP to materialize full weight tensors on-demand.

cards.front: What is the "reduce-scatter" collective?
cards.back: Each chip starts with the full tensor; result is summed and then sharded back so each chip ends up with 1/N of the reduced result. Pairs with all-gather to form an all-reduce.

cards.front: What is the identity: all-reduce = all-gather ∘ reduce-scatter?
cards.back: Two-step ring all-reduce: first reduce-scatter (each chip ends up with 1/N of the sum), then all-gather (every chip gets the full sum). Total volume is 2(N−1)/N · B.

cards.front: For TPU v4, what is the peak BF16 throughput per chip?
cards.back: Approximately 275 BF16 TFLOPs.

cards.front: For TPU v5p, what is the peak BF16 throughput per chip?
cards.back: Approximately 459 BF16 TFLOPs.

cards.front: What is the difference between v5e and v5p?
cards.back: v5e = efficiency tier (smaller pods, lower cost / TFLOP, inference + small training). v5p = performance tier (large pods, highest TFLOPs/chip, large-model training).

cards.front: What was new in Trillium (TPU v6) vs v5p?
cards.back: ~4.7× peak compute per chip vs v5e; doubled HBM bandwidth and capacity; SparseCore upgrades; better perf/$ for embedding-heavy workloads.

cards.front: What is "SparseCore" on TPUs?
cards.back: A specialized on-chip accelerator for embedding lookups and sparse gathers — operations the dense MXU handles badly. Critical for ranking/recommendation models.

cards.front: Why is the SparseCore separated from the MXU rather than integrated?
cards.back: Sparse lookups have wildly different memory-access patterns (random, latency-bound) from dense matmul (sequential, bandwidth-bound). Different silicon optimum for each.

cards.front: What is the "memory wall" problem for neural-network accelerators?
cards.back: Compute throughput grows faster than memory bandwidth each generation, so kernels become increasingly bandwidth-bound. Mitigations: bigger on-chip SRAM, op fusion, lower precision (BF16/FP8/INT8), and shorter dependency chains.

cards.front: What is "FP8" and where does it appear in modern TPUs?
cards.back: An 8-bit floating-point format (variants E5M2 and E4M3) introduced in Trillium-era TPUs and H100-class GPUs. Halves memory and compute cost vs BF16, with accuracy losses manageable for many inference + some training workloads.

cards.front: Why might E4M3 be preferred for weights and E5M2 for activations in FP8 training?
cards.back: Weights have a narrower dynamic range and benefit from extra mantissa (E4M3 = 4 exp bits, 3 mantissa). Activations and gradients have wider range and need more exponent (E5M2). Pairing them per tensor is standard.

cards.front: What is "quantization-aware training" (QAT)?
cards.back: Train the network while simulating the low-precision arithmetic that will be used at inference, so the weights adapt to the quantization error instead of suffering it after the fact.

cards.front: What is "post-training quantization" (PTQ)?
cards.back: Train in BF16/FP32 normally, then quantize weights (and optionally activations) to INT8 / FP8 using a calibration set. Cheaper than QAT but accuracy loss is larger for sensitive models.

cards.front: What is "kernel fusion" vs "graph fusion" in XLA?
cards.back: Kernel fusion = collapsing a chain of ops into one MXU/VPU program; graph fusion = at the HLO level, rewriting the computation graph (e.g., reorder + combine matmuls) before code generation. Both reduce HBM round-trips.

cards.front: What is the FLOP count of a (M, K) × (K, N) matrix multiplication?
cards.back: 2 · M · K · N floating-point ops (one multiply + one add per element of the output).

cards.front: For a (1024, 1024, 1024) BF16 matmul, how many BF16 ops and how many bytes touched (no reuse)?
cards.back: Ops = 2·1024³ ≈ 2.15 GFLOPs. Bytes (3 matrices × 1024²×2 bytes) ≈ 6.3 MB. Operational intensity ≈ 340 FLOPs/byte → compute-bound on v4.

cards.front: Why is batch size a tuning knob on TPU training?
cards.back: Larger batch → better MXU utilization (less pipeline-fill waste) and amortized ICI all-reduce cost, but it also changes the optimizer dynamics (LR scaling rules apply).

cards.front: What is the "linear LR scaling rule" when batch size grows by k?
cards.back: Multiply the learning rate by k (and use a brief warmup) to keep the per-example gradient noise scale roughly constant. Holds up to a model-dependent critical batch size.

cards.front: Why does TPU pricing favor staying within ICI rather than spanning DCN?
cards.back: ICI bandwidth ≈ 10–100× DCN bandwidth, and DCN traffic adds variable latency. Jobs that fit in one slice are both faster and cheaper per step.

cards.front: What is "host offload" used for on TPU training?
cards.back: Spill activations or optimizer state from HBM to host DRAM over PCIe when HBM is the bottleneck. Pays a bandwidth penalty (PCIe ≪ HBM) but unblocks larger models.

cards.front: What is a typical reason a TPU job runs slower than its roofline predicts?
cards.back: Idle MXU cycles caused by HBM stalls, ICI synchronization (all-reduce), padding waste, or recompile thrash. Profile with XLA's HLO and step-time breakdown before assuming the model is the bottleneck.

cards.front: What is "JAX pjit" for?
cards.back: A wrapper around XLA SPMD that automatically partitions arrays according to a declared sharding spec, hiding most of the manual collective calls. The default high-level API for multi-chip training.

cards.front: What is "asynchronous dispatch" in JAX, and why does it matter on TPUs?
cards.back: JAX returns futures from compiled functions; the actual work runs on TPU asynchronously while Python continues. Benchmarking requires `.block_until_ready()` or you'll time only the dispatch, not the compute.

cards.front: What is "XLA recompile thrash" and how do you avoid it?
cards.back: When input shapes change frequently, XLA recompiles the program each time → minutes of overhead per step. Fix: pad to fixed bucket shapes and reuse compiled programs.

cards.front: What is the typical end-to-end latency budget for a token in transformer inference on TPU v5?
cards.back: A few ms for small models (< 7 B params, single chip), tens of ms for 70 B class with model parallelism, hundreds of ms for frontier models with multi-slice serving. Dominated by HBM bandwidth for the per-token weight reads.

cards.front: What is "KV-cache" and why is it the biggest HBM consumer in long-context inference?
cards.back: The cached Key and Value projections for every previous token in every layer. Size = 2 × layers × heads × head_dim × seq_len × dtype_size. For 70 B / 128k context this dwarfs the model weights themselves.

cards.front: For a 70 B model with 80 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim=128, BF16, and 128k context, what is the KV-cache per request?
cards.back: 2 · 80 · 8 · 128 · 128000 · 2 bytes ≈ 42 GB. That's why long-context serving requires aggressive sharding, paged-attention, and/or KV quantization.

cards.front: What is "paged attention"?
cards.back: A KV-cache management scheme borrowed from OS virtual memory — store the cache in fixed-size blocks across HBM, look them up via a page table. Lets the scheduler pack many concurrent requests without contiguous-allocation waste.

cards.front: What is "speculative decoding"?
cards.back: Use a small fast draft model to propose N tokens, then verify all N in a single forward pass of the big model. If most are accepted, latency drops by ~Nx without quality loss.

cards.front: What is "tensor-parallel" sharding for a matmul?
cards.back: Split the matmul along its contraction (K) or output (N) dimension across chips. Each chip computes a partial result; an all-reduce or all-gather combines them. Standard for serving large transformer layers.

cards.front: What is the failure mode if you tensor-parallel a matmul whose N is smaller than the chip count?
cards.back: Each chip ends up with a tiny slice that under-utilizes its MXU (M, N, K must each be ≥ 128 for full BF16 utilization). The all-reduce overhead then dwarfs the actual compute → throughput collapses.

cards.front: Why is profiling a TPU job a different exercise than profiling a CPU program?
cards.back: No general-purpose instruction trace — XLA must emit specialized counters (MXU utilization, HBM read/write bytes, ICI bytes). Tools: XProf / TensorBoard profiler / xla_dump. Don't sample with Python time; use device timings.

cards.front: What does "MXU utilization" actually measure in XProf?
cards.back: The fraction of cycles the MXU was performing useful MAC ops (vs. waiting on HBM, ICI, padding, or VPU). Target ≥70%; below 40% means the workload is severely memory-bound or shape-misaligned.

cards.front: What is the canonical first thing to check when a TPU training job is slow?
cards.back: Step-time breakdown in XProf: how much time was MXU active, how much was HBM read/write, how much was ICI all-reduce, how much was host (input pipeline). Optimize the largest slice first.

cards.front: What is "input-pipeline starvation"?
cards.back: The TPU sits idle waiting for the next batch because the host CPU + tf.data / grain pipeline can't keep up. Fix: bigger prefetch buffer, parallel parsing, on-device data loading where possible.

cards.front: What is the "two-axis sharding" pattern in modern LLM training?
cards.back: One mesh axis for data parallelism (gradient all-reduce), another for model/tensor parallelism (within-step collectives). A 2-D mesh (e.g., 8 × 32 chips) gives both, and you tune the split per model size.

cards.front: Reference paper for TPU v1?
cards.back: Jouppi et al., "In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit," ISCA 2017.

cards.front: Reference paper for TPU v4?
cards.back: Jouppi et al., "TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings," ISCA 2023.

cards.front: Canonical paper on the systolic-array idea (long before Google TPUs)?
cards.back: H. T. Kung & Charles E. Leiserson, "Systolic Arrays (for VLSI)," 1979 (CMU). Foundational for understanding the dataflow style TPUs revived.

cards.front: Canonical paper introducing bfloat16?
cards.back: Internal Google work, popularized via Wang et al., "BFLOAT16: The secret to high performance on Cloud TPUs," Google Cloud Blog 2019. The format itself predates that — Intel's Nervana used it earlier.

cards.front: Recommended free hands-on resource for learning TPU programming?
cards.back: JAX tutorial series + Google Cloud TPU Research Cloud (TRC) free tier. Pair with Karpathy-style "build it from scratch" exercises (4×4 systolic in NumPy first, then JAX pmap on real TPUs).

cards.front: What is the bfloat16 layout vs IEEE float16?
cards.back: bfloat16: 1 sign + 8 exponent + 7 mantissa (same dynamic range as fp32). fp16: 1 sign + 5 exponent + 10 mantissa (higher precision, narrow range). TPUs prefer bf16 because gradients don't underflow.

cards.front: Why does bfloat16 dominate over fp16 on TPUs?
cards.back: Same exponent width as fp32 → no loss scaling needed during training. fp16's narrow range causes underflow on gradient products.

cards.front: What is FP8 used for on modern TPUs/GPUs?
cards.back: Lower-precision training and inference. Two flavors: E4M3 (more precision, used in forward pass) and E5M2 (more range, used for gradients in backward).

cards.front: What is "loss scaling" and when do you still need it?
cards.back: Multiplying the loss by a constant (e.g., 1024) before backward so small gradients don't underflow in fp16. Not needed with bf16; required with fp16; sometimes needed at extreme batch sizes in fp8.

cards.front: What is INT8 KV-cache quantization?
cards.back: Storing the K and V tensors in 8-bit integers (with per-channel scales) instead of bf16 — cuts cache memory ~4×, almost no quality loss for most models. Critical for long-context inference.

cards.front: What is the "memory wall" in attention?
cards.back: Attention scales O(N²) in sequence length for both compute AND memory; the memory cost dominates first because HBM is the bottleneck, not the MXU. FlashAttention is the standard fix.

cards.front: What does FlashAttention do at one level?
cards.back: Computes attention tile-by-tile in SRAM with online softmax — never materializes the full N×N attention matrix in HBM. Reduces memory from O(N²) to O(N).

cards.front: What is the formula for self-attention?
cards.back: softmax(Q · Kᵀ / √d_k) · V, where Q, K, V are (N × d_k) projections of the input. The 1/√d_k term keeps softmax temperature stable as d_k grows.

cards.front: What is multi-head attention?
cards.back: Run attention h times in parallel with different learned Q/K/V projections, then concatenate. Lets the model attend to different subspaces simultaneously. Cost = roughly same as single head with d_k/h.

cards.front: What is GQA (Grouped Query Attention)?
cards.back: Heads share K and V across groups (e.g., 8 query heads → 1 KV head). Cuts KV cache by group_factor× at small quality cost. Standard in Llama-3, Gemma, etc.

cards.front: What is MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention)?
cards.back: DeepSeek's trick: project K and V into a low-rank latent shared across heads. KV cache drops ~10× vs MHA; reconstructed on-the-fly per head. State-of-art for long context.

cards.front: Formula for the KV-cache memory of one layer?
cards.back: 2 × batch × seq_len × num_kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_elem. Multiply by num_layers for the model. Memorize this — it dominates inference RAM.

cards.front: Why is LLM inference "two workloads in one kernel"?
cards.back: Prefill = compute-bound (large batched matmul over the prompt). Decode = memory-bound (one token at a time, must reload weights and KV from HBM each step).

cards.front: What is "continuous batching" in serving?
cards.back: Dynamically inserting new requests into the decode batch as old ones finish, instead of waiting for a fixed batch to complete. ~3–5× throughput on serving systems like vLLM / JetStream.

cards.front: What is speculative decoding?
cards.back: A small draft model proposes k tokens; the big model verifies them all in one parallel forward pass. Accept matches, restart at first mismatch. ~2–3× decode speedup.

cards.front: What is the goal of "tiling" on TPU?
cards.back: Slice big matmuls into SRAM-sized tiles (typically 128×128 per MXU lane) so each tile fits in fast memory and gets reused across many MAC ops. This is how you actually hit high MFU.

cards.front: Why does the TPU prefer matrix shapes that are multiples of 128?
cards.back: The MXU is a 128×128 systolic array; non-multiples cause padding waste. Always pad batch/feature dims to 128 (or 8 for some smaller MXUs).

cards.front: What is "double buffering" in TPU tiling?
cards.back: Overlap HBM→SRAM transfers of the next tile with MXU work on the current tile. Hides memory latency so the MXU never idles. XLA does this automatically when shapes allow.

cards.front: What is SparseCore on TPU?
cards.back: A separate compute unit optimized for embedding-table lookups (recommenders, retrieval). Handles the irregular gather/scatter pattern the MXU is bad at.

cards.front: What is "embedding sharding" in recommender models?
cards.back: Splitting huge embedding tables (TB-scale) across SparseCores by row hash; lookup → all-to-all → dense network. Standard for ads/recsys at scale.

cards.front: What is XProf?
cards.back: Google's TPU profiler — captures op-level timing, HBM bandwidth, MXU utilization, communication overlap. Open via TensorBoard plugin. The first thing you reach for when MFU is low.

cards.front: What does "MFU" tell you specifically?
cards.back: Model FLOPS Utilization = (useful FLOPs you performed) / (peak FLOPs the chip can do in the same wall time). >50% on training = excellent; <20% = something is wrong (often memory-bound, bad shapes, or comms-bound).

cards.front: What is "goodput" vs throughput?
cards.back: Throughput counts every step. Goodput counts only steps that produced useful, retained progress (excluded: hung steps, recovered failures, recomputed work). Goodput is the honest metric at scale.

cards.front: Top three reasons MFU is low on a fresh TPU training run?
cards.back: (1) Shapes not multiple of 128, (2) too small a batch per chip (memory-bound), (3) comms not overlapped with compute (check ICI usage in XProf).

cards.front: What is Orbax?
cards.back: JAX's sharded checkpoint library. Writes each shard from the chip that owns it, in parallel, to GCS. Async by default so training doesn't stall.

cards.front: What is a "jaxpr"?
cards.back: JAX's intermediate representation — a typed, traced graph of pure functions. Produced by jax.make_jaxpr(fn) after one trace. Sits between Python and StableHLO.

cards.front: What is StableHLO?
cards.back: A versioned, stable serialization of XLA's HLO IR. Lets you save a compiled program today and recompile it years later. The framework-agnostic on-disk format.

cards.front: What is "shard_map" in JAX?
cards.back: Per-device explicit SPMD — you write the function as if running on one chip with sharded inputs, JAX adds collectives at the boundaries. More predictable than pjit's automatic partitioner.

cards.front: What is a "mesh" in JAX?
cards.back: A logical n-D grid of devices with named axes (e.g., ('data', 'model')). Sharding specs reference axis names, decoupling math from physical topology.

cards.front: Difference between DCN and ICI?
cards.back: ICI = Inter-Chip Interconnect, within a pod, ~µs latency, hundreds of GB/s. DCN = Data Center Network, across pods (multislice), ~ms latency, ~tens of GB/s. Hierarchical collectives use both.

cards.front: What is "optical circuit switching" on TPU v4+?
cards.back: Each pod has reconfigurable optical switches that can change the 3D-torus topology in software — pick the best wiring for your workload's collective pattern. Why TPU v4's paper title says "optically reconfigurable."

cards.front: What is JetStream?
cards.back: Google's open-source LLM inference engine for TPU — continuous batching, prefill/decode disaggregation, paged KV cache. The reference serving stack.

cards.front: What is "prefill/decode disaggregation"?
cards.back: Run the prefill workload on one pool of chips (compute-bound, good MFU) and decode on a separate pool (memory-bound, low MFU). Different pools sized differently. Major recent serving win.

cards.front: What is the typical training recipe for fault recovery on a pod?
cards.back: Async checkpoint to GCS every N steps + elastic restart via the JAX coordinator. On chip failure, restart from last checkpoint on a smaller slice; resume when hardware recovers.

cards.front: Cardinal rule for picking TPU vs GPU?
cards.back: Throughput at scale & JAX/XLA shop → TPU. Single-node max flexibility & PyTorch shop → GPU. The compiler & sharding story is what actually differs, not raw FLOPs.
